clinician.trajectory_summary: A 5-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of a transverse cutaneous 'split' on the plantar aspect of the right third toe associated with serous discharge that progressively elongated circumferentially over 1 month to involve the dorsal aspect. Physical examination revealed a distinct 'split' sign (boundary between normal skin and affected crusted skin overlying osteolysis) on the third toe with circumferential involvement, serous discharge without bony spicule discharge, and shortening of the distal phalanges of the 2nd, 4th, and 5th toes. Sensation and peripheral pulses were normal. X-ray of the right foot confirmed progressive osteolysis: complete resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the 5th toe, complete resorption of the terminal phalanx of the 4th toe, partial resorption of the terminal phalanx of the 3rd toe, and partial resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the 2nd toe. Extensive laboratory workup (CBC, renal function, liver function, PTH, ANA, RF, anti-CCP, CRP, fasting glucose, calcium, phosphate, albumin, thyroid function) was normal, ruling out infections, connective tissue disorders, endocrine disorders, and lipid storage diseases. No clinical or radiographic findings of inflammatory/rheumatic disorders such as psoriatic arthritis were present. Notably, the mother reported similar demarcation lines on the 2nd, 4th, and 5th toes of her right foot with durations of 3 months, 1 year, and 2 years respectively, which disappeared before shortening of those toes, suggesting a familial pattern. The clinical and radiologic features—distinct 'split' sign with circumferential involvement, progressive osteolysis on imaging, maternal history of similar lesions with prior resolution before shortening, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses—are consistent with Intrauterine Amputation Sequence (IAO), a rare congenital condition characterized by fibrous bands causing circumferential constriction and progressive auto-amputation of digits.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Inflammatory/rheumatic disorder (e.g., psoriatic arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: No clinical or radiographic findings of inflammatory/rheumatic disorders; normal inflammatory markers (CRP); normal RF and anti-CCP tests
Normal PTH, calcium, phosphate, and thyroid function tests
Normal liver function tests, albumin, and comprehensive metabolic panel
No history of trauma reported; distinct 'split' sign with demarcation line characteristic of congenital fibrous band, not traumatic injury
No history of Raynaud phenomenon; normal peripheral pulses; no evidence of vascular compromise on examination

remaining_uncertainties: Clinical course and final outcome of the active third toe split (whether it progressed to auto-amputation or resolved without amputation)
Histopathology or tissue biopsy findings confirming the fibrous band mechanism (not documented in available evidence)
Imaging findings of the left foot for comparison and determination of unilateral versus bilateral involvement
Detailed maternal diagnosis confirmation and extended family history (paternal side, siblings, cousins)
Genetic testing or inheritance pattern documentation
Specific management or surgical intervention provided for the active lesion
